description: Congratulations on reaching the end of the curriculum! This final assessment checks the same skills as the pre-test: Big-O notation and tracing how code executes, across all AlgoBlocks modules.

questions.code:
x = 6
y = 2
x = x + y
y = x - y
x = x - y
print(x, y)
questions.question: Trace this code line by line. What is printed, and what is the cost?
options: 6 2: the values stay the same, and the cost is O(1)
8 6: x keeps the sum, and the cost is O(1)
2 6: the values are swapped using a fixed number of steps, so O(1)
2 6: the values are swapped, but the cost is O(n)
questions.explanation: x = 8, then y = 8 - 2 = 6, then x = 8 - 6 = 2. The values are swapped without a temporary variable, and every step is a constant-time statement: O(1).

questions.question: The Python panel shows a loop that runs n / 2 times with one constant-time statement in its body. What complexity does the analyzer report?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: n / 2 passes are still proportional to n. The constant factor 1/2 is dropped, so the class is O(n), not O(log n), which needs the size to be halved each pass.

questions.question: Trace the variable best through the loop. What is printed, and what is the cost?
options: 4: best keeps the first value, and the time is O(n) with O(1) extra space
7: best keeps the last value, and the time is O(n) with O(1) extra space
9: best holds the largest value seen, and one pass is O(n) time with O(1) extra space
9: best holds the largest value, but copying into best needs O(n) extra space
questions.explanation: best becomes 4, then 9, and stays 9 because 2 and 7 are not larger. One pass over n items is O(n) time, and only one variable is stored: O(1) extra space.

questions.question: A function that does O(log n) work is called on every pass of a loop that runs n times. What is the overall time complexity?
options: O(log n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n + log n)
questions.explanation: n passes × O(log n) per call = O(n log n). The cost per call is multiplied by the number of calls.

questions.question: Trace the nested loop. What is printed, and how does the work grow with n?
options: 6: only the outer loop is counted, so O(n)
21: the inner loop runs 6+5+4+3+2+1 times, which is about n²/2, so O(n²)
36: the inner loop always runs 6 times, so O(n²)
21: the inner loop runs 6+5+4+3+2+1 times, but that grows as O(n)
questions.explanation: For i = 0..5 the inner loop runs 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 times = 21. A triangular count is about n²/2, and Big-O drops the 1/2, giving O(n²).

questions.question: Trace the index reads. What is printed, and what is the cost?
options: 85: arr[2] is 15 and arr[-1] is 55, and both are direct reads in O(1)
71: arr[2] is treated as the second item (8), and the cost is O(1)
64: arr[-1] is treated as the second-last item (34), and the cost is O(1)
85: arr[2] is 15 and arr[-1] is 55, but each read costs O(n)
questions.explanation: Zero-based index 2 is the third item, 15, so 15 * 2 = 30. arr[-1] is the last item, 55. 30 + 55 = 85. Index access is a direct jump, so O(1).

questions.question: Algorithm A reverses a list by building a new reversed list. Algorithm B swaps items inside the original list. What are their auxiliary space complexities?
options: A uses O(1); B uses O(n)
Both use O(n)
A uses O(n); B uses O(1)
Both use O(1)
questions.explanation: A allocates a second list of n items: O(n) extra space. B only needs a couple of index variables and a swap, so its extra space is O(1).

questions.question: A program must check 1,000 times whether a value was already seen. Which storage gives the better total time, and why?
options: A list: scanning is faster than hashing for every size
A set: about 1,000 × O(1) lookups, instead of 1,000 × O(n) with a list
A list: lookups in a list are O(1)
Neither: both give the same total time
questions.explanation: Each set lookup is O(1) on average, so the total grows with the number of checks. With a list, each check may scan n items, so the total becomes about 1,000 × n.

questions.question: Which operation on a Python list of n items takes O(1) time?
options: Reading the length with len(arr)
Checking membership with x in arr
Copying the list with arr[:]
Finding the largest item with max(arr)
questions.explanation: len(arr) reads a stored value. Membership checks, copies and max() all have to visit up to n items, so they are O(n).

questions.code:
arr = []
for i in range(1, 5):
    arr.append(i * i)
print(arr, len(arr))
questions.question: Trace the loop. What is printed, and what is the cost of n appends?
options: [0, 1, 4, 9] 4: i starts at 0, and n appends cost O(n) in total
[1, 4, 9, 16, 25] 5: range(1, 5) includes 5, and n appends cost O(n) in total
[1, 4, 9, 16] 4: each append is O(1) amortized, so n appends cost O(n) in total
[1, 4, 9, 16] 4: every append recopies the list, so n appends always cost O(n²)
questions.explanation: i runs 1, 2, 3, 4, so the list is [1, 4, 9, 16] with length 4. Appends are O(1) amortized, so building the list is O(n).

questions.code:
arr = [6, 2, 9, 4]
target = 5
steps = 0
for x in arr:
    steps += 1
    if x == target:
        break
print(steps)
questions.question: Trace the search for a value that is not in the list. What is printed, and which case is this?
options: 1: the loop stops at the first item: the best case, O(1)
2: the loop stops halfway: the average case, O(log n)
4: the target is absent, so all n items are checked: the worst case, O(n)
4: all items are checked, but the worst case is O(1)
questions.explanation: 5 never appears, so there is no break and all 4 items are checked. A missing target forces a full scan: worst case O(n).

questions.question: The list is in reverse order. What is printed, and what does it show about bubble sort?
options: [1, 2, 3, 4] 3: it needs n − 1 swaps, so the worst case is O(n)
[1, 2, 3, 4] 6: a reversed list needs n(n−1)/2 swaps, so the worst case is O(n²)
[4, 3, 2, 1] 0: no swaps are needed, so the worst case is O(1)
[1, 2, 3, 4] 6: it needs n(n−1)/2 swaps, but the worst case is O(n)
questions.explanation: All 6 pairs are out of order, so 4·3/2 = 6 swaps. The count grows as n(n−1)/2, which is O(n²).

questions.question: A brute-force method checks every pair among n items. About how many checks does it make, and what is the class?
options: About n checks: O(n)
About 2ⁿ checks: O(2ⁿ)
About n(n−1)/2 checks: O(n²)
About log n checks: O(log n)
questions.explanation: The number of pairs among n items is n(n−1)/2, which has an n² term. Dropping the constant leaves O(n²).

questions.question: An algorithm's best case is Ω(1) and its worst case is O(n). Which statement is true?
options: Its running time is always constant
Its running time is always linear
Its running time depends on the input and lies between constant and linear
Its running time is quadratic in the worst case
questions.explanation: Ω(1) says it can finish in constant time on some inputs, and O(n) says it never needs more than linear time. The actual time depends on the input.

questions.code:
s = ""
for ch in "abc":
    s = ch + s
print(s)
questions.question: Trace the loop. What is printed, and why can this pattern become costly?
options: cba: each step builds a new string, so the copying can add up to O(n²) in total
abc: the letters are added in order, and the loop is always O(1)
cba: Python edits the string in place, so the loop is O(log n)
cb: the last letter is skipped, and the loop is O(1)
questions.explanation: s becomes "a", then "ba", then "cba". Each step creates a new string that copies the old one, so n steps can cost about 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n²) character copies.

questions.question: A list is unsorted and you only need to search it once. Which approach has the lower time complexity?
options: Linear search at O(n), because sorting first costs O(n log n)
Sort then binary search, because O(log n) is always faster
Binary search directly, because it works on any list
They cost the same, O(log n)
questions.explanation: Binary search needs sorted data, and sorting costs O(n log n). For a single search, one O(n) linear scan is cheaper overall.

questions.code:
arr = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]
target = 4
lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
probes = []
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    probes.append(arr[mid])
    if arr[mid] == target:
        break
    elif arr[mid] < target:
        lo = mid + 1
    else:
        hi = mid - 1
print(probes)
questions.question: Trace the binary search. Which values are probed, and what does that show about its complexity?
options: [2, 4]: items are checked from the start, so O(n)
[8, 4]: the range is halved on each probe, so O(log n)
[8, 6, 4]: the probe moves one item at a time, so O(n)
[8, 4]: the range is halved on each probe, but it is O(n)
questions.explanation: mid = 3 → 8 > 4, so hi = 2. Then mid = 1 → 4 is found. Only two probes, because each one cuts the remaining range in half: O(log n).

questions.code:
left = [1, 2, 3]
right = [4, 5, 6]
i = j = 0
merged = []
comparisons = 0
while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
    comparisons += 1
    if left[i] <= right[j]:
        merged.append(left[i])
        i += 1
    else:
        merged.append(right[j])
        j += 1
merged += left[i:] + right[j:]
print(merged, comparisons)
questions.question: Trace this merge step of merge sort. What is printed?
options: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] 6: every item is compared once, so merge sort is O(n²)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] 3: merging is one pass, about n work per level, which gives O(n log n) overall
[4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3] 3: the lists are swapped, so merge sort is O(n)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] 5: five comparisons are made, so merge sort is O(log n)
questions.explanation: 1, 2 and 3 are all smaller than 4, so 3 comparisons empty the left list. The right list is then appended as is. Merging stays about n per level: O(n log n) in total.

questions.question: Quick sort always picks the first element as its pivot and receives an already sorted list. What is the running time, and why?
options: O(n²): the pivot is the smallest item, so each partition removes only one item
O(n log n): the pivot always splits the list in half
O(n): the list is already sorted, so no work is needed
O(log n): the pivot is the middle item
questions.explanation: With a sorted list and a first-item pivot, one side is always empty, so there are n levels of partitioning, each costing up to n: O(n²).

questions.question: Trace the recursion. What is printed, and what is the time complexity of f(n)?
options: 5: n roughly halves on each call, so the depth is O(log n)
20: there is one call for each unit of n, so the time is O(n)
4: the base case adds nothing, and the time is O(log n)
5: n roughly halves on each call, but there are two calls each time, so O(n)
questions.explanation: f(20) → f(10) → f(5) → f(2) → f(1). f(1) returns 1 and four returns add 1 each: 5. The base case stops the recursion, and the halving gives O(log n) depth.

questions.question: A greedy algorithm makes one pass over n items that are already sorted, doing constant work per item. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: One pass with constant work per item is O(n). The O(n log n) only appears when the data must also be sorted first.

questions.code:
acts = [(0, 2), (1, 4), (3, 5), (5, 7), (6, 9)]
acts.sort(key=lambda a: a[1])
last = 0
chosen = []
for s, e in acts:
    if s >= last:
        chosen.append((s, e))
        last = e
print(chosen)
questions.question: Trace the activity selection. Which activities are chosen, and what is the total cost?
options: [(0, 2), (1, 4), (3, 5), (5, 7)]: overlapping activities are kept, so O(n log n)
[(0, 2), (3, 5), (5, 7)]: an O(n log n) sort followed by an O(n) pass gives O(n log n)
[(0, 2), (6, 9)]: only the first and last are chosen, so O(n)
[(0, 2), (3, 5), (5, 7)]: an O(n log n) sort followed by an O(n) pass gives O(n²)
questions.explanation: Take (0,2); skip (1,4) because 1 < 2; take (3,5); take (5,7) because 5 ≥ 5; skip (6,9) because 6 < 7. The sort dominates the single pass: O(n log n).

questions.code:
coins = [5, 4, 1]
amount = 8
count = 0
for c in coins:
    while amount >= c:
        amount -= c
        count += 1
print(count)
questions.question: Trace the greedy coin choice. What is printed, and what does it show?
options: 4: greedy takes 5+1+1+1, but 4+4 needs only 2 coins, so greedy is not always optimal
2: greedy takes 4+4, so greedy is always optimal
4: greedy takes 4+4+0+0, so greedy is optimal here
8: greedy uses eight 1-coins, so greedy is optimal only for 1-coins
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 5 first (3 left), skips 4, then takes three 1-coins: count 4. The optimal answer is 4 + 4 = 2 coins, so greedy is fast but not always optimal.

questions.question: A greedy algorithm inserts n items into a heap (each O(log n)) and then removes n items (each O(log n)). What is the total time complexity?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: n inserts and n removals, each costing O(log n), give 2n log n steps. Dropping the constant leaves O(n log n).

questions.code:
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 67
used = []
for c in coins:
    while amount >= c:
        amount -= c
        used.append(c)
print(used)
questions.question: Trace the greedy coin selection. What is printed?
options: [25, 25, 10, 5, 1, 1]: it always takes the largest coin that still fits, a locally best choice
[10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 5, 1, 1]: it always takes the smallest coin that fits
[25, 25, 10, 5, 1]: it stops before the last 1 is taken
[25, 25, 5, 5, 5, 1, 1]: it skips the 10-coin
questions.explanation: 67 → 25 (42) → 25 (17) → 10 (7) → 5 (2) → 1 (1) → 1 (0). At each step greedy takes the largest coin that still fits.

questions.question: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci (O(2ⁿ)) a good candidate for dynamic programming?
options: It recomputes the same subproblems many times, so storing results removes repeated work
It splits the input into independent halves
It always makes the locally best choice
It already runs in O(n), so DP only saves memory
questions.explanation: fib(n) calls fib(n−1) and fib(n−2), and these calls repeat the same smaller values. Storing each result once turns O(2ⁿ) into O(n).

questions.question: Trace this memoized Fibonacci. What is printed (the value and the number of calls), and what is the time complexity?
options: 13 41: every subproblem is recomputed, so the calls grow as O(2ⁿ)
21 13: fib(7) is 21, and the calls grow linearly: O(n)
13 13: each subproblem is solved once, so the calls grow linearly: O(n)
13 7: only one call is made per value, so the time is O(log n)
questions.explanation: fib(7) = 13. Memoization makes 13 calls (a plain recursive fib(7) makes 41). Each value is computed once and then reused, so time is O(n).

questions.question: Which problem is a better fit for dynamic programming than for divide and conquer?
options: Sorting a list with merge sort, because the subproblems overlap
Counting the ways to climb n stairs using steps of 1 or 2, because the subproblems overlap
Binary searching a sorted list, because the subproblems overlap
Finding the maximum of a list, because the subproblems overlap
questions.explanation: The number of ways to reach stair n reuses the answers for stairs n−1 and n−2, which repeat. Sorting, binary search and maximum have independent or single subproblems.

questions.code:
weights = [2, 1, 3]
values = [4, 2, 7]
W = 5
dp = [0] * (W + 1)
for i in range(len(weights)):
    for w in range(W, weights[i] - 1, -1):
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weights[i]] + values[i])
print(dp)
questions.question: Trace this one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack. What does dp print, and what are the costs?
options: [0, 2, 4, 7, 9, 11]: one array of size W+1 gives O(W) space with O(n·W) time
[0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10]: the best value is the sum of values per weight, so O(W) space with O(n·W) time
[0, 2, 4, 7, 9, 13]: an item is counted twice in dp[5], so O(n·W) space
[0, 2, 4, 7, 9, 11]: one array of size W+1 gives O(n·W) space with O(W) time
questions.explanation: Each item updates dp from right to left so it is used at most once. The final dp[5] = 11 (items of weight 2 and 3). One array of W+1 values gives O(W) space; n items × W cells give O(n·W) time.

questions.question: A 0/1 knapsack dp table has n + 1 rows and W + 1 columns, and each cell is filled once. What is its time complexity, and what is decided in each cell?
options: O(n·W): each cell chooses between taking or skipping the current item
O(2ⁿ): each cell tries every subset of items
O(n + W): each cell is filled by adding one item
O(log W): each cell halves the remaining capacity
questions.explanation: There are about n × W cells and each takes constant time to compare 'skip the item' with 'take the item'. That is O(n·W), much better than 2ⁿ for moderate W.

questions.question: Which statement about the worst-case time of backtracking with pruning is true?
options: It is always O(n) because pruning removes every bad branch
It is always O(log n) because each step halves the choices
It can still be exponential or factorial, even though pruning often makes it much faster
It is always O(1) because the answer is found immediately
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts branches that fail early, but inputs exist where almost nothing is pruned, so the worst-case class (for example O(2ⁿ) or O(n!)) stays.

questions.question: Trace this decision tree (3 choices per level, depth 2). What is printed, and how does it grow?
options: 5: the tree has 3 + 2 leaves, so linear growth in the depth
9: branching factor 3 and depth 2 give 3² leaves, so the growth is bᵈ in the depth
2: only one leaf is counted per level, so O(n)
9: branching factor 3 and depth 2 give 3² leaves, but it grows as O(log n)
questions.explanation: The first level has 3 branches and each branch has 3 more: 3 × 3 = 9 leaves. In general b^d leaves, so the tree grows exponentially with depth.

questions.question: Queens are in rows 0 and 1 (columns 0 and 2). Trace the safety check for row 2. What is printed?
options: []: every column is attacked, so the search reaches a dead end and must backtrack
[1, 3]: only the same column is checked, so columns 1 and 3 are safe
[3]: only diagonals of the first queen are checked, so column 3 is safe
[0, 2]: the queens' own columns are always safe
questions.explanation: Column 0 and column 2 share a column with a queen. Column 1 is diagonal to the row-1 queen, and column 3 is diagonal to it as well. No safe place remains, so the algorithm must undo the last queen and try another column.

questions.code:
result = []
path = []
def pick(start):
    if len(path) == 2:
        result.append(path[:])
        return
    for i in range(start, 4):
        path.append(i + 1)
        pick(i + 1)
        path.pop()
pick(0)
print(result[:3], len(result))
questions.question: Trace this combination generator (choose 2 of 4). What is printed?
options: [[1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4]] 6: pop() undoes each choice so the next one starts from a clean path
[[1, 2], [2, 1], [1, 3]] 6: the order of the items is also changed
[[1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4]] 4: only four pairs exist
[[1, 2], [3, 4], [1, 3]] 6: the pairs are made from unused items only
questions.explanation: The path [1,2] is saved, pop() removes 2 and the loop tries 3: [1,3], then [1,4]. Choosing 2 of 4 gives 6 pairs. Without pop() the path would keep stale items.

questions.question: How does the number of permutations change when n goes from 5 to 6?
options: It adds 1, from 120 to 121, which shows linear growth
It doubles, from 120 to 240, which shows exponential growth
It multiplies by 6, from 120 to 720, which shows factorial growth
It stays the same, because the extra item adds nothing
questions.explanation: 6! = 6 × 5! = 720. Each extra item multiplies the count by the new n, which is factorial growth, faster than doubling.
